subject: Evaluating connectivity: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN (proposal & pilot)
messages:
From: Sarah Lopez <sarah.lopez@acmeanalytics.com>
To: karthik_iyer <karthik.iyer@redwoodai.com>
Cc: Peter Chang <pchang@acmeanalytics.com>, netops@acmeanalytics.com
Date: 2026-10-25T09:03:00-07:00
Subject: Evaluating private deployment connectivity options

Hi Karthik,

Thanks for taking a look. We're kicking off design for a Private deployment of Redwood in our AWS account and trying to settle on a connectivity pattern. Short background: we are HIPAA + SOC2, operate across us-east-1 and us-west-2, target sustained ~200 RPS during peak with spikey bursts to 800 RPS. Latency sensitivity: 95th token latency under 200ms is desirable, but we prioritize reliability and auditability over micro-optimizations right now.

Options on the table: VPC peering across accounts, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints / NLB proxy), and a site-to-site VPN from our on-prem gateways. Primary constraints for us:
- Need predictable source egress IPs for allowlists
- Audit trail / flow logs for compliance (retain 1 year)
- Minimal ops burden — we'd prefer Redwood-managed where reasonable
- Ability to scale without large refactors as traffic grows

Could you outline recommended tradeoffs and a practical pilot approach? We have a hard deadline to pick a pilot path by 2026-11-01.

Appreciate any short checklist and proposed next steps (firewall rules, required IAM, expected outage windows).

Best,
Sarah
Sarah Lopez
Head of Platform Engineering, Acme Analytics
From: karthik_iyer <karthik.iyer@redwoodai.com>
To: Sarah Lopez <sarah.lopez@acmeanalytics.com>

Subject: Re: Evaluating private deployment connectivity options

Hi Sarah — thanks for the clear constraints.

High-level guidance (short):
- Site-to-site VPN: fastest to stand up for a PoC from your on-prem (low engineering lift), gives immediate egress IP control (your firewall side), but tends to be higher latency and brittle under heavy burst traffic unless we put in HA tunnels and active/passive routers. Good for initial functional validation and compliance evidence.

- VPC Peering: great for high-bandwidth, low-latency east-west traffic inside AWS (same region). Caveats: peering is not transitive (so cross-account/multi-region topology can get complex), and you lose fine-grained interface-level identity (we can't enforce per-service PrivateLink policies). Also requires routing changes and potentially SNAT if CIDR overlaps exist. Recommended when you own both VPCs or want maximum throughput without proxy hops.

- PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint / NLB proxy): recommended when you want strong isolation, no routing changes in the customer's VPC, and a stable endpoint that can be allowlisted. It supports AWS PrivateLink across accounts and regions (with regional endpoints) and plays nicely with customer NACLs/security groups. Performance is generally good for request volumes like yours if we front with NLB and tune keepalive/batching; costs are higher than peering but operationally simpler for customers and easier to meet compliance (no peering routes to manage).

Preliminary recommendation: two-stage approach
1) PoC (week of 2026-11-01): Stand up an HA S2S VPN between your on-prem and a dedicated Redwood test VPC. This gives you quick proof of connectivity, allows you to validate audit logs and egress behavior, and keeps the initial ops bar low.
2) Production: Evaluate PrivateLink with an NLB + proxy in each region where you need low-latency. If you need very high throughput within the same AWS account, consider peering for intra-region heavy data paths and PrivateLink for the control/ingest plane.

Immediate MOP / firewall rules (PoC):
- Allow outbound TCP 443 (TLS) from your NAT/egress IPs to our test VPN endpoints (I’ll provide exact IPs once we schedule)
- For PrivateLink pilot: allow inbound from our interface endpoint ENIs (we'll provide security group ranges) or allowlisted DNS names as needed

I've attached a short checklist and a cost outline for the three paths (connectivity-decision-checklist.pdf, approx-cost-outline.xlsx).

If that direction sounds acceptable I can loop in Ben and Kim to scope a short test plan (latency/throughput/observability) and a simple firewall rule list you can hand to NetOps.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Lead Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: karthik_iyer <karthik.iyer@redwoodai.com>

Date: 2026-10-26T09:04:00-07:00
Subject: Fwd: Evaluating private deployment connectivity options — proposed pilot scope

Folks — forwarding Sarah's request and my note. Key ask: quick PoC by 11/01 using S2S VPN; longer-term production leaning toward PrivateLink + NLB proxy per region, with peering reserved for heavy intra-region data flows.

Proposed pilot checklist (open items in []).
- Redwood test VPC and VPN endpoints: create 2 AZ-redundant tunnels in us-east-1; provide customer IPSec PSK and peer IPs. (owner: networking infra, ETA: 10/29)
- Observability: enable VPC flow logs + integration to their SIEM (they want 1-year retention). We need a template for log export and retention SLAs. (owner: kimberly_park)
- Latency/throughput tests: generate steady 200 RPS workload + 3x burst test to 800 RPS; capture p50/p95/p99 token and request latency. Pass criteria: p95 request latency < 250ms for PoC. (owner: ben_carter)
- Security/compliance artifact pack: outline of network architecture diagrams, key rotation plan, and audit steps for SOC2 (I think they'll need HLD + flow logs). (owner: jonas_weber)
- Firewall rules for customer: minimal list for PoC (we'll provide source IPs). (owner: karthik_iyer)

Architectural notes worth calling out for design review:
- PrivateLink + NLB-proxy approach: place an NLB in Redwood account fronting the inference cluster, terminate TLS at the NLB or at an internal proxy based on customer preference. Use PrivateLink interface endpoints in customer VPCs that point to the NLB. Advantages: no route table changes in customer, stable DNS, easier identity/rate-limiting per endpoint. Downside: per-ENI cost and cross-AZ bandwidth costs.

- Peering considerations: if customer asks for peering, we should only recommend for same-account or carefully mapped cross-account peering with strict route filtering; watch CIDR overlaps and transitive traffic.

- VPN constraints: avoid using VPN for long-term production without HA BGP and redundant carriers — it's operationally heavier than PrivateLink for scale.

Please review and flag anything I missed. If we agree, I'll send a compact MOP and the firewall/peering details to Sarah so NetOps can action it.
